blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper from Google researchers that addresses the challenge of measuring the causal impact of marketing activities or feature rollouts. The authors propose using Bayesian Structural Time-Series (BSTS) models to estimate what would have happened without an intervention (the counterfactual) and compare it to the observed outcomes. The key insight is to use historical data, contemporaneous control time series, and Bayesian priors to build a predictive model that can estimate the true causal effect. The approach is illustrated with a real-world example where the model accurately predicted the counterfactual and estimated an additional 88,400 clicks due to an advertising campaign, closely matching results from a conventional control. The paper also highlights the flexibility of BSTS models in handling trend, seasonality, and dynamic regression coefficients, and their applicability even without dedicated control regions by leveraging publicly available industry-related time series data.
paper_title: Inferring Causal Impact Using Bayesian Structural Time-Series Models
paper_abstract: Quantifying cause and effect relationships is an important problem in many domains. The gold standard solution is to conduct a randomised controlled trial. However, in many situations such trials cannot be performed. In the absence of such trials, many methods have been devised to quantify the causal impact of an intervention from observational data given certain assumptions. One widely used method are synthetic control models. While identifiability of the causal estimand in such models has been obtained from a range of assumptions, it is widely and implicitly assumed that the underlying assumptions are satisfied for all time periods both pre- and post-intervention. This is a strong assumption, as synthetic control models can only be learned in pre-intervention period. In this paper we address this challenge, and prove identifiability can be obtained without the need for this assumption, by showing it follows from the principle of invariant causal mechanisms. Moreover, for the first time, we formulate and study synthetic control models in Pearl’s structural causal model framework. Importantly, we provide a general framework for sensitivity analysis of synthetic control causal inference to violations of the assumptions underlying non-parametric identifiability. We end by providing an empirical demonstration of our sensitivity analysis framework on simulated and real data in the widely-used linear synthetic control framework.
